The sarangi is a short-necked bowed instrument of South Asian traditional music, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71. It is hollowed from a single piece of red cedar, the body has a box-shaped resonance chamber divided into three cavities, goatskin covers the lower part, and it carries three main gut strings and several sympathetic strings. The player bows with a horsehair bow and stops the strings with the fingernail, the edge of the nail and the surrounding flesh, dusted with talcum powder. Its repertoire is traditionally closely tied to vocal music, and a concert solo can unfold a raga and its accelerating sections; the Nepali version is a four-string folk instrument, mostly played by Gaine or Gandarbha people.
薩朗吉琴為南亞傳統弓弦樂器，尼泊爾版本為四弦民間樂器，多由蓋內或甘達爾巴族群演奏: The sarangi is a traditional bowed instrument of South Asia; the Nepali version is a four-string folk instrument, mostly played by Gaine or Gandarbha people, with a repertoire more folk-based than India's. Around the twentieth century the harmonium and the violin became substitutes because they are easier to play. In Pakistan performance has declined since the 1980s, which is connected with the deaths of several masters and with the religious radicalisation under Zia-ul-Haq's rule.
薩朗吉琴為弓拉短頸弦鳴樂器，初學先以馬尾弓拉奏三條主腸弦，按弦不用指尖，而以指甲: The sarangi is a bowed short-necked chordophone. To begin, bow the three main gut strings with a horsehair bow; the strings are not stopped with the fingertips but with the fingernail, the edge of the nail and the surrounding pad, and the fingers are dusted with talcum powder so that they slide on the bone or ivory platform of the neck. A smaller body is steadier to hold. In playing, the tuning of the sympathetic strings has to be understood at the same time, and vibrato and slides are practised according to vocal tradition, along with the repertoire's words, its speeds and its structure.
薩朗吉琴琴身以整塊紅杉木雕刻，呈箱形；下共鳴腔覆山羊皮膜，膜上置厚皮革條支撐象形: The sarangi body is carved from a single piece of red cedar in a box shape; the lower resonance chamber is covered with a goatskin membrane, on which a thick leather strip supports the shaped bridge, usually made of camel or buffalo bone. The three main strings are gut, and the sympathetic strings, about thirty-five to thirty-seven, are steel or brass, held up by hollow ivory or bone beads; some instruments also use goat-gut strings. The neck has an ivory or bone platform for the fingers to slide on, and the bow is a heavy horsehair bow. The materials of the other parts are not stated in the source.
薩朗吉琴見於南亞傳統音樂，曲目多與聲樂相關。獨奏會有時可完整呈現拉格，由自由引子: The sarangi appears in the traditional music of South Asia, and its repertoire is mostly bound up with singing. A solo recital can sometimes set out a whole raga, from the free alap through the jor and jhala to a bandish, following vocal conventions such as khyal and thumri. The Nepali sarangi is more folk-based and is usually played by Gaine or Gandarbha people; it also appears in the Nepali folk song "Resham Firiri", accompanied by sarangi and madal drum.
薩朗吉琴音色溫潤而富有人性化特質，具有獨特的沙啞感與深邃的鼻音色彩，彷彿捕捉了人: The sarangi's timbre is warm and human in character, with a distinctive hoarseness and a deep nasal colour, as if it caught the finest emotional shades of the voice. Its range is wide, running from the middle to the upper register, and it can carry a broad span of dynamics. With its bowing technique the strings and the body resonate fully, and the tone is round and penetrating. Its greatest strength is expression — it can imitate all the ornaments of singing, such as vibrato and slides, giving a piece a flowing linear quality. Against the bright, exciting violin the sarangi is darker and more inward; against the heavy, low cello it is more flexible and intimate, and it is the most song-like string instrument in Indian traditional music.
